Dear Secretary Reese:

        On May 21, 2026, Horizon Merger Sub, Inc. (“Horizon Merger Sub”) and The AES
Corporation (“AES”) on behalf of each of its subsidiaries that is or will be a public utility (the
“AES Public Utilities” or “AES Applicants,” and the AES Applicants together with Horizon
Merger Sub, the “Applicants”) submitted an application (the “Application”) in the captioned
docket requesting authorization pursuant to Sections 203(a)(1) and 203(a)(2) for a transaction
(“Transaction”) in which Horizon Merger Sub will merge with and into AES, with AES continuing
as the surviving corporation. 1 Applicants explained therein that the Transaction requires, among
other authorizations and consents, prior approval from the Public Utility Commission of Ohio
(“PUCO”). On September 17, 2026, PUCO issued an order approving the Transaction (the “PUCO
Approval”). In accordance with Section 33.2(i) of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s
(the “Commission”) regulations, 2 Applicants hereby provide the attached copy of PUCO’s order.

 THE DAYTON POWER AND LIGHT
 COMPANY D/B/A AES OHIO, HORIZON

 PARENT, L.P., AND HORIZON MERGER
 SUB, INC. TO APPROVE AN INDIRECT
 CHANGE IN CONTROL OF AES OHIO.

                                  FINDING AND ORDER


                        Entered in the Journal on September 17, 2026


                                       I.   SUMMARY

       {¶ 1}    The Commission approves the application filed by The Dayton Power and
Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio, Horizon Parent, L.P., and Horizon Merger Sub, Inc. to
approve a change in control of AES Ohio, adopting the modifications made herein.

                                     II.    DISCUSSION

       {¶ 2}    The Dayton Power and Light Company d/b/a AES Ohio (AES Ohio or the
Company) is an electric light company and a public utility as defined by R.C. 4905.03 and
R.C. 4905.02, respectively. The Company is also an electric utility as defined in R.C. 4928.01.
As such, AES Ohio is subject to the jurisdiction of this Commission.

       {¶ 3}    Under R.C. 4905.402(B)(1), no person shall acquire control, directly or
indirectly, of a domestic electric utility or a holding company controlling a domestic electric
utility unless that person obtains the prior approval of the Commission. Pursuant to R.C.
4905.402(B)(2), to obtain approval of a change in control, the person seeking the approval
shall file an application with the Commission, containing such information as the
Commission may require, “demonstrating that the acquisition will promote public
convenience and result in the provision of adequate service for a reasonable rate, rental, toll,
or charge.” If, after review of the application and any necessary hearing, the Commission
is satisfied that approval of the application will promote public convenience and result in
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                                      -2-

the provision of adequate service for a reasonable rate, the Commission shall approve the
application and make such order as it considers proper. If the Commission fails to issue an
order within 30 days of the filing of the application, or within 20 days of the conclusion of
any hearing held, the application shall be deemed approved by operation of law. R.C.
4905.402(B)(2).


A. Procedural History


       {¶ 4}      On March 5, 2025, in Case No. 24-960-EL-MER, the Commission issued a
Finding and Order approving AES Ohio’s joint application with AES Ohio Holdings, Inc.,
AES Ohio Investments, Inc., and Astrid Holdings LP1 (Astrid Holdings). As a result, Astrid
Holdings acquired indirect equity interests in the Company which totaled approximately
30 percent.

       {¶ 5}      On April 10, 2026, AES Ohio, Horizon Parent, L.P. (Horizon), and Horizon
Merger Sub, Inc. (Merger Sub) (collectively, Joint Applicants), filed an application for the
Commission’s approval of an indirect change in control of AES Ohio (Application).

       {¶ 6}      Horizon is a Delaware limited partnership controlled by investment vehicles
affiliated with one or more funds, accounts, or other entities managed or advised by Global
Infrastructure Management, LLC, which operates under the trading name Global
Infrastructure Partners (GIP), a part of BlackRock, Inc. (BlackRock). Furthermore, Merger
Sub, a Delaware corporation, is currently a direct and wholly owned subsidiary of Horizon.

       {¶ 7}      By Entry dated May 8, 2026, to permit for an investigation and the
Commission’s full consideration of whether approval of the Application will promote
public convenience and result in the provision of adequate service for a reasonable rate




1 Astrid Holdings is a Delaware limited partnership and wholly owned subsidiary of Caisse de dépôt et
  placement du Québec (CDPQ), which manages public and private pension funds in the Province of Québec.
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                            -3-

under R.C. 4905.402(B)(2), the administrative law judge (ALJ) suspended the Application
such that it would not be deemed approved by operation of law and set forth a procedural
schedule. Specifically, the ALJ directed that motions to intervene would be filed by June 8,
2026; Staff’s review and recommendation would be filed by July 8, 2026; initial comments
regarding the Application or Staff’s review and recommendation were due by July 29, 2026;
and reply comments were due by August 12, 2026.

      {¶ 8}    Timely motions to intervene in this proceeding were filed by the City of
Dayton (the City), the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel (OCC), Citizens’ Utility Board of Ohio
(CUB Ohio), and Clinton County Residents for Responsible Development (CCRRD). The
ALJ granted intervention to the parties on July 9, 2026.

      {¶ 9}    On June 5, 2026, OCC filed a motion to consolidate this matter with AES
Ohio’s three-year rate plan, pending in Case Nos. 25-958-EL-AIR, et al. (the TYRP
Proceeding). On June 22, 2026, the Company filed a memorandum in opposition to the
motion to consolidate, to which OCC filed a reply on June 29, 2026. In the TYRP Proceeding,
the evidentiary hearing took place on August 4, 2026, during which the evidentiary record
was closed upon the conclusion of the hearing for the Commission’s consideration of the
matter. Thus, the Commission finds this motion to be a moot issue. The request to
consolidate the matter is denied.

      {¶ 10}   On July 9, 2026, Staff filed its review and recommendations (Staff Report)
accompanied by a motion for leave to file the same out of time. By Entry on July 9, 2026, the
ALJ accepted the Staff Report as timely and accordingly extended the comment deadlines
by one day.
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                                          -4-

       {¶ 11}     On July 30, 2026, and on August 13, 2026, Joint Applicants, CCRRD, the City,
CUB Ohio, and OCC filed timely initial and reply comments, respectively.2


B. Summary of Application


       {¶ 12}     On March 1, 2026, AES Corporation (AES Corp.), Horizon, and Merger Sub
entered into an Agreement and Plan of Merger (Merger Plan). According to the Application,
Merger Sub was formed for the purpose of merging with and into AES Corp., with AES
Corp. as the surviving corporation. The Application explains that AES Corp. holds, through
DPL LLC3, 70 percent indirect equity interests in AES Ohio. All remaining equity interests
in AES Ohio are indirectly held by CDPQ through Astrid Holdings. See In re The Dayton
Power and Light Co. d/b/a AES Ohio, Case No. 24-960-EL-MER (2024 Merger Case).
Immediately prior to the closing of the merger transaction (Transaction), the purchasers (as
identified below) will fund their pro rata share of the merger consideration in exchange for
the voting common stock of Merger Sub. Upon the execution of the Transaction, AES Ohio
would be jointly owned by the following purchasers: (1) 36.625 percent by investment funds
and vehicles controlled or managed by affiliates of GIP; (2) 33.375 percent by investment
funds, vehicles and/or separate accounts managed and/or advised by controlled affiliates
of EQT AB4 (together with its affiliates, EQT); (3) 10 percent by investment funds and

  expedited treatment, any memoranda contra or replies in response to the motion should be filed pursuant
  to Ohio Adm.Code 4901-1-12(B) for the Commission’s consideration.

3 DPL LLC is an Ohio limited liability company and a holding company, not subject to the Commission’s
  regulation as a public utility under R.C. 4905.02. See 2024 Merger Case.

4 EQT AB is publicly traded on the Stockholm Nasdaq (ticker symbol EQT). EQT is a long-term, active

  energy transition, and other core infrastructure projects in North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific.
  (Application at 5.)
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                                               -5-

vehicles controlled or managed by Qatar Investment Authority5 (QIA); and (4) 20 percent
by investment funds and vehicles owned by California Public Employees’ Retirement
System6 (CalPERS) under a passive ownership structure in which CalPERS’ interests will be
controlled or managed by GIP.              Upon closing of the Transaction, investment funds or
vehicles of the GIP, EQT, CalPERS, and QIA (collectively, the Consortium) are expected to
directly own AES Corp. Moreover, the Application states that GIP and EQT will have co-
governance rights in AES Corp. (Application at 3-5.)

        {¶ 13}    The Application states that the Transaction will continue AES Ohio’s
significant community support. As part of the Merger Plan, AES Ohio makes several
commitments, such as those enumerated under Section 6.06:

                  a. Customer and Community Benefits

                         i. AES Ohio will not recover from its customers the acquisition
                             premium of the transactions contemplated by the Merger Plan.

                         in its service territory.

                    iv. AES Ohio will continue to comply with Ohio’s corporate separation
                         law and rules.

                b. Local and Management Commitments

                      i. AES Ohio will maintain its headquarters in Dayton, Ohio.

                     ii. AES Ohio’s board of directors will have at least one member from
                         Ohio, and the CEO/President of AES Ohio will be a member of AES

                         subject to changes to account for voluntary departures or

(Application at 7-8; Merger Plan at 77-78.) Also, the Merger Plan includes commitments
regarding base salary or wage rates, target incentive compensation opportunities, and
employee benefits for the first year following the Transaction (Merger Plan at 81).

       {¶ 14}   Additionally, the Application indicates that AES Ohio shall remain subject
to the Commission’s jurisdiction under Ohio law and the Commission’s rules, such that the
Commission’s authority to regulate the Company’s rates, tariffs, terms of service, and
service quality will not change in any way. The Application states that the Transaction will
not affect the Company’s rates, rate base, tariffs, terms of service, or service quality, and nor
will it affect the Company’s local management, employees, or operations. Additionally, the
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                                -7-

Application submits that AES Ohio will continue to have the managerial, technical, and
financial capabilities to provide safe and reliable electric utility service to more than half a
million customers in West Central Ohio. As such, AES Ohio will still own, operate, and
maintain its distribution and transmission systems to provide service and will continue to
facilitate competitively-sourced default generation service pursuant to R.C. 4928.121, et seq.
Relatedly, the Application confirms that the Company will remain a separate public utility,
and all of its activities will continue to be accounted for separately. Furthermore, the
Application states that the Company will continue to invest prudently in utility assets to
meet its customers’ needs. According to the Application, the Transaction will enhance AES
Ohio’s access to long-term capital from its parent company and thus allow AES Ohio to
invest in critical energy infrastructure assets, deliver reliable energy solutions for customers,
and create long-term value for all stakeholders, including its workforce and local
communities. The Application explains that the Consortium and their members take a long-
term view with their investments, with returns dependent on AES Ohio’s customer
performance over the long term by maintaining high reliability, strong credit, and affordable
rates, dependent upon consistent, multi-year investment. (Application at 6-8.)

       {¶ 15}   The Application also indicates that after the announcement of the
Transaction, Moody’s issued a Ratings Action on March 2, 2026, which stated “[t]he ratings
and outlooks of AES subsidiaries, including . . . Dayton Power and Light Company (Baa 3
stable) . . . remained unchanged.” Relatedly, on March 3, 2026, S&P Global issued a Tear
Sheet stating that “AES Ohio’s credit quality was not affected by the Transaction.” Also, on
March 4, 2026, in response to the announcement of the proposed transaction, Fitch Ratings
issued a Rating Action Commentary “affirming the rating of AES Ohio as BBB-/stable.”
(Application at 9.)


C. Summary of Staff Report


       {¶ 16}   With regard to the Transaction, the Staff Report analyzes the promotion of
public convenience and impact on customers and performs a managerial review, technical
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                                 -8-

review, and financial review.      The Staff Report states that the public convenience is
measured by whether the service is necessary, suitable, fitting, and beneficial. Overall, the
report recommends that the Commission find that the Transaction meets these criteria. Staff
emphasizes that new service is not contemplated in this proceeding, but rather the
continuance of AES Ohio’s service as is. Staff believes that the Transaction will not create
redundant services, as they are necessary to the community in the present and future. Staff
reports that the Transaction is only a change in control of ownership for AES Ohio, not a
change in its operations. As such, the Company will continue to provide electric utility
service, where the Consortium will contribute significant experience with long-term
infrastructure investments, as well as significant financial resources. Accordingly, Staff
recommends that the Consortium is a suitable owner for the Company. (Staff Report at 3.)

       {¶ 17}   The Staff Report states that the communities served by AES Ohio will
experience very little impact as a result of the change in AES Ohio’s ownership, since the
Transaction does not contemplate any changes to local management, rates, terms of service,
tariffs, or quality of service. Staff asserts that customers should see no transaction costs
recovered through the rates, and they will not be required to adjust to the change in
ownership. As such, Staff indicates that customers will not see any changes to the call center,
to their digital experience, bill formats, or field experiences. Staff therefore believes that the
Transaction has little to no foreseeable drawbacks for AES Ohio, and it may provide the
Company with increased opportunities for investing in energy infrastructure delivering
solutions and better customer outcomes. Staff concludes that the benefits of an active,
investing ownership outweighs the foreseeable drawbacks and result in the provision of
adequate service to customers. (Staff Report at 4.)

       {¶ 18}   Staff also certifies that the Transaction should not impact AES Ohio’s
managerial and technical capabilities to provide adequate service. Upon its review of the
Company’s data request responses, Staff verifies that the Company intends to keep all of its
technical employees. Moreover, Staff believes that GIP and EQT, as experienced long-term
infrastructure investors, will provide strategic guidance and share best practices with the
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                              -9-

Company. Relatedly, Staff anticipates that the Transaction would provide AES Corp.
greater financial flexibility as a private company to advance its strategy and meet the needs
of AES Ohio’s customers by providing reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy solutions.
In support, Staff notes that the Consortium is funding the proposed merger with equity, and
without any incremental debt, which the ratings agencies (Moodys, S&P, and Fitch Ratings)
perceive as “credit supportive.” Staff also notes that the Transaction is not expected to
impact AES Ohio’s or DPL LLC’s existing debt instruments. Furthermore, upon its financial
review, Staff reports that the Consortium’s rapport with a broad set of lenders should
provide adequate funding to supplement internally generated funds that will be reinvested
in AES Corp.’s subsidiaries in support of future capital investments. The Staff Report thus
recommends that the Transaction is reasonable and should not adversely impact Ohio
customers. Staff recommends that AES Ohio be required to provide updates to Staff on any
changes in systems, policies, and procedures for at least three years. (Staff Report at 5-7.)


D. Public Comments


       {¶ 19}   As part of the considerations in this matter, the Commission takes
administrative notice of relevant feedback provided during the local hearings in AES Ohio’s
TYRP Proceeding and filings made under the case docket’s Public Comments section.
During the local hearings, individuals raised concerns about the Transaction and its impacts
on rate affordability; excessive earnings to the detriment of the ratepayer; speculation of
possible conflicts of interests related to private equity ownership of a public utility; a need
for improved transparency to ratepayers; a shift in customer prioritization to large load
customers, including data centers; impacts on service/grid reliability; need for investment
in the current grid without transaction costs related to the acquisition; the Consortium’s lack
of familiarity with the local community; and overall disapproval of the proposed
Transaction. Additionally, some individuals requested an additional local hearing for the
Transaction. In re the Dayton Power and Light Co. d/b/a AES Ohio, Case No. 25-958-EL-AIR, et
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                                  - 10 -

al., Pub. Transcript (July 9, 2026) at 25, 41-42, 69; Pub. Transcript (July 16, 2026) at 12-13, 16-
17, 35, 37-38, 45-46, 53, 57, 59-63, 71, 78-79, 87, 91, 94, 106, 109-110,116-117, 120, 129-130, 133.

       {¶ 20}   In addition to the comments delivered during the TYRP Proceeding’s local
public hearings, the Commission received eight filings in this proceeding (at the time of this
Finding and Order). On June 1, 2026, the President of the Utility Works Union of America
Local 175 (the Union), John Arnett, wrote that the Transaction provides AES Ohio
“enhanced” access to long term capital, which will allow the Company to build critical
energy infrastructure. Additionally, Mr. Arnett’s letter indicates that he has experienced
several acquisitions with various utilities, and this is the first time he was asked by the
purchasing entities about ways they could help the Union better serve AES Ohio’s
customers. Additionally, on August 18, 2026, Adam Murka, President of Fidelity Strategies
in Montgomery County, Ohio, submitted a comment in support of the Transaction, praising
the opportunity for AES Ohio to have greater financial flexibility to invest in newer
infrastructure. Also, on August 28, 2026, a public individual, Chris Sanford, submitted a
comment in favor of the Transaction, as it presents an opportunity for AES Ohio to support
continued investment in Ohio’s energy infrastructure, while protecting the interests of the
communities AES Ohio serves.

       {¶ 21}   On July 9, 2026, the Commission also received a public comment in
opposition to the Transaction from Ms. Jessica Sharp, a community organizer and member
of Wilmington Residents for Responsible Development. Similar to concerns voiced during
the TYRP Proceeding local hearings, Ms. Sharp emphasizes that residential customers
should not become the financial backstop of infrastructure expansion in response to large
load customers, including data centers. Additionally, two other public comments from
“Anonymous” and Mr. Robert Butts were submitted in opposition to the Transaction.

       {¶ 22}   Furthermore, we recognize that on August 12, 2026, State Representative
Tristan W. Rader of the 13th House District filed correspondence which asks the
Commission to hold public hearings in this proceeding.                   Representative Rader’s
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                            - 11 -

correspondence states that due to the pending TYRP Proceeding and forecasted data center
load growth, the Company is facing fundamental questions regarding cost allocation for
new infrastructure, reliability of service, and long-term operations as a result of the
Transaction. Similarly, on August 28, 2026, State Representative Tom Young of the 37th
House District, submitted correspondence that declares Ohio customers should not bear
increased costs or reliability risks resulting from AES Ohio’s potential new owners. Within
his correspondence, Representative Young poses multiple questions for the Commission to
clarify and consider when rendering its final decision in this proceeding.


E. Party Comments


       {¶ 23}   In initial comments, the intervening parties assert that the Staff Report is
insufficient to varying degrees and request that the Commission require ring-fencing
provisions to be implemented by the Company as part of the Transaction.

       {¶ 24}   CCRRD, CUB Ohio, and the City raise concerns over the risks associated
with the Transaction, including its impact on the local Dayton-area economy and the
residential ratepayers. The City states that while the Merger Plan indicates that AES Ohio’s
headquarters will continue to be in Dayton, Ohio, it does not clearly define the facility,
duration, level of operations, or protections against future relocation or material reduction
in headquarters operations. Relatedly, the City emphasizes that it has a particular interest
in ensuring the Transaction does not result in workforce reductions that would diminish
employment opportunities for residents, reduce municipal tax revenues, or compromise
AES Ohio’s ability to provide adequate service. The City highlights that AES Corp.’s
predecessor defined workforce protections in the prior change-of-control proceeding and
the City wants to see similar protections in this case. The City also asks the Commission to
require AES Ohio to maintain 1) its headquarters in the City of Dayton for at least 20 years;
2) the existing senior leadership and key operational decision-making in the City for at least
20 years (subject to ordinary-course departures, retirements, and terminations for cause or
performance); and 3) at least 90 percent of the baseline Dayton-area workforce working in
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                             - 12 -

city limits for 20 years following the Transaction’s closing, with the baseline based on the
average number of Dayton-area employees from calendar years 2020 through 2022.
Furthermore, the City encourages an expansion of economic development and affordability
programming, as well as an increase in charitable spending. The City also asks that AES
Ohio streamline the vetting and approval process for public infrastructure projects. (City
Initial Comm. at 2-7.)

       {¶ 25}    CCRRD takes issue with the Transaction’s related impacts on large-scale
data center development and the build out of transmission infrastructure and associated
grid stress. CCRRD emphasizes that it is not trying to litigate cost allocation. Instead,
CCRRD is concerned about the Transaction’s associated risk, in which the cost and the
forecasted cost of large-load driven build would be shifted to residential customers.
(CCRRD Initial Comm. at 7-8.)

       {¶ 26}    CCRRD, the City, and CUB Ohio agree that the Application and Merger Plan
do not offer firm commitments. Specifically, CCRRD alleges that the Application and
Merger Plan have gaps in their assurances for an equity floor, retained-earnings protection,
and docketed compliance reporting As such, CCRRD and CUB Ohio request that AES Ohio
be required to submit annual compliance reports in the case docket on topics including the
Company’s capital structure, affiliate financing arrangements, local operational headcount,
and upstream dividend distributions docketed with the Commission. The City asks the
Commission to require annual reporting for any commitments that the Commission relies
upon for its approval. (City Initial Comm. at 7; CCRRD Initial Comm. at 5; CUB Ohio Initial
Comm. at 7-8.)

       {¶ 27}    In response, Joint Applicants submit that the Application and Merger Plan
include a robust series of commitments that address customer and community benefits,
local and management considerations, corporate separation protections, continued
investment in AES Ohio’s territory, and an agreement not to recover transaction costs from
ratepayers. Particularly, Joint Applicants state that they are sensitive to the City’s concerns
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                            - 13 -

and reiterate the commitment to keep the Company’s headquarters in Dayton, Ohio. On
the other hand, Joint Applicants indicate that requiring AES Ohio to maintain at least 90
percent of the baseline Dayton-are workforce working in city limits for 20 years would be
unrealistic and overly restrict AES Ohio’s decision-making to the extent that it could impact
utility affordability. However, Joint Applicants assert that the Transaction is not the kind
of utility merger that could result in headcount reductions resulting from the consolidation
of operations with another utility, as there is no planning or possibility of consolidation of
AES Ohio’s operations. Furthermore, Joint Applicants emphasize that the Merger Plan
includes a one-year period of post-Transaction workforce protections for AES Ohio
employees. Joint Applicants add that the City’s specific requests regarding the approval
process for public infrastructure projects and waiver of interconnection costs are outside the
scope of its process. Nonetheless, Joint Applicants note that AES Ohio will continue to be
diligent and collaborate with the City on all of its development projects. (Joint App. Reply
Comm. at 6-10.)

       {¶ 28}   Further, Joint Applicants explain that no transaction costs or acquisition
premiums are being passed on to ratepayers, as agreed to in the TYRP Proceeding’s Joint
Recommendation and Stipulation (TYRP Stipulation), which shall be verifiable during the
rate case’s annual true-up proceeding. Joint Applicants also recognize that CCRRD, OCC,
CUB Ohio, and the City raise concerns over future rates, merger savings, and the allocation
of any financial benefits for the Transaction. Again, Joint Applicants argue that these issues
are specifically addressed in the unopposed TYRP Stipulation, and that these concerns are
matters of ratemaking that are not relevant to this proceeding.           Nonetheless, Joint
Applicants indicate that the intervenors’ remaining issues shall be resolved in the pending
TYRP Proceeding, and that the Commission should not prejudge such inquiries raised
during this change-in-control proceeding. Joint Applicants assert that the Commission has
consistently recognized that change-in-control proceedings have reserved future rate issues
for ratemaking cases, where a complete record can be developed, citing to In re The East Ohio
Gas Company d/b/a Dominion Energy Ohio and Enbridge Elephant Holdings, LLC, Case No.
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                             - 14 -

23-972 GA-UNC, Finding and Order (Mar. 6, 2024); In re Notice of a Merger Involving the
Parent Company of Vectren Energy Delivery of Ohio, Inc., Case No. 18-1027-GA-UNC, Finding
and Order ¶ 13 (Jan. 30, 2019). (Joint App. Reply Comm. at 10-12.)

       {¶ 29}   Joint Applicants also note concerns over potential refinancing involved with
the Transaction is now a moot point, since a consent was obtained from the lender group

F. Commission Conclusion


       {¶ 36}   R.C. 4905.402(B) states that no person shall acquire control, directly or
indirectly, of a domestic electric utility or a holding company controlling a domestic electric
utility unless that person obtains the Commission’s prior approval. Furthermore, according
to R.C. 4905.402(B), to obtain approval the applicant shall file an application with the
Commission demonstrating that the acquisition will promote public convenience and result
in the provision of adequate service for a reasonable rate. As described in the Application,
the proposed Transaction will result in a change in the control of a holding company
controlling a domestic electric utility. Therefore, the Commission is statutorily required to
determine whether approval of the Application will promote public convenience and result
in the provision of adequate service for a reasonable rate.

       {¶ 37}   Upon our review of the Application and the attached Merger Plan, Staff
Report, the comments submitted for consideration by the intervenors, and public testimony
and submitted comments, we find that the Transaction would promote the public
convenience and result in the provision of adequate service for a reasonable rate. At the
outset of this determination, the Commission notes that Staff evaluated public convenience
by whether the service being provided is, and will continue to be, necessary, suitable, fitting
and beneficial. Additionally, Staff reviewed several AES Ohio data request responses to
support its recommendation. On balance, CCRRD and CUB Ohio argue that Staff’s analysis
was insufficient in analyzing whether the Transaction would advance or further public
convenience. We recognize that members of the public, legislators, and intervenors raise
concerns regarding the Transaction’s long-term effects, including large load and data center
cost allocation, continuation of ratepayer protections, service reliability, and the relationship
with Dayton, Ohio and the Company’s surrounding service territory; relatedly, OCC, CUB-
Ohio, and CCRRD ask the Commission to enforce ring-fencing provisions to improve
consumer protections. However, the Commission is satisfied by the thoroughness of Staff’s
review and endorses the overall conclusion that the customers served by AES Ohio will
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                              - 20 -

experience very little impact due to the change in the Company’s ownership, as the
Transaction does not contemplate any changes to local management, rates, terms of service,
tariffs, or quality of service.

       {¶ 38}    In support of our conclusion, we emphasize that this proceeding does not
contemplate a new service, but rather a continuation of AES Ohio’s existing services. As
such, customers should not see any noticeable changes to their interactions with the utility.
For instance, no modifications will be made to the call center, customer digital experience,
bill formats, or field experiences. Additionally, the Staff Report verified that customers shall
not experience transaction costs recovered through rates. (Staff Report at 4; Application at
6-7.) The Commission also understands that there are concerns over the retention of the
Company’s headquarters in Dayton, Ohio, and whether AES Ohio will continue its
longstanding community relationships and employment opportunities.              However, the
Merger Plan states that AES Ohio shall remain headquartered in the City of Dayton and it
requires AES Ohio to maintain its recent level of economic development and charitable
contributions, including contributions made on its behalf, in its service territory. Relatedly,
we determine that the change in ownership will not impact AES Ohio’s management and
technical expertise. Notwithstanding changes made in the ordinary course of business, the
Company shall maintain its current senior management team. Moreover, Joint Applicants
have proactively addressed employee transitions associated with the Transaction, where the
Merger Plan includes employee protection provisions effective for one year following the
Transaction. (Application at 7-8; Merger Plan at 77-78.) Moreover, while the Commission
cannot compel AES Ohio to commit to certain employee contractual obligations, it would
be our expectation for Joint Applicants to extend the applicable time frame during which
these employee protections are in place, in furtherance of its continued symbiotic
relationship with the City and the surrounding community. See, e.g., In re the Application of
The AES Corporation, Dolphin Sub, Inc., and The Dayton Power and Co., Case No. 11-3002-EL-
MER, Finding and Order (Nov. 22, 2011). Additionally, we emphasize that the Transaction
does not contemplate a utility merger that could result in a personnel reduction due to
 26-435-EL-MER                                                                            - 21 -

combining workforces with another utility. Therefore, there appears to be no imminent
cause or reason for a significant fluctuation in AES Ohio’s Dayton-based work force, and
Joint Applicants also represent that there are no plans for a consolidation of operations and
nor would it be feasible due to the Transaction.

       {¶ 39}   Additionally, we do not diminish the concerns voiced by members of the
public and the General Assembly, or by intervening parties. However, we emphasize that
the scope of this proceeding is not a catch-all for all utility-related matters and that some
issues are better addressed by the Commission in other types of proceedings. For instance,
the City’s request for commitments from AES Ohio regarding future infrastructure projects
or waiver of interconnection costs is inapplicable to this proceeding. However, we are
satisfied with Joint Applicants’ response that AES Ohio will continue to collaborate with the
City regarding all of its development projects. Accordingly, we emphasize that it is essential
for the Company to maintain its rapport as a good partner and neighbor in the Dayton, Ohio
area. Similarly, concerns over large load customers and data center costs are matters of
ratemaking and are thus outside of the scope of this case. The question of cost allocation or
cost-shifting related with the Company’s large load customers, including data centers, is
much better suited for the consideration of AES Ohio’s TYRP Proceeding, which involves a
lengthy evidentiary record specifically on proposed rate designs for the years of 2027
through 2029. Moreover, we refrain from prejudging the merits of the TYRP Proceeding,
but we note that the TYPR Stipulation submitted in that proceeding proposes a Data Center
Tariff that could address CCRRD’s concerns. The Commission’s decision in this proceeding
is well informed of the Company’s rate trends—since the latest rate case (Case No.
24-1009-EL-AIR, et al.) was adjudicated in 2025—and we are aware of the Company’s
proposed commitments and projections submitted in the pending TYRP Proceeding.

       {¶ 40}   Furthermore, a directive for ring-fencing provisions would be redundant in
this matter, due to the applicable provisions established in the 2024 Merger Case.
Accordingly, unless expressly allowed by the Commission, AES Ohio’s new debt or credit
agreements will not include change-of-control or cross-default clauses tied only to other

AES Ohio debt. 2024 Merger Case, Finding and Order (Mar. 5, 2025) Order at ¶ 17, 26-27.
Additionally, the Company will have separate credit facilities, will not engage in
intercompany lending or borrowing, will maintain its own independent stand-alone credit
rating, and will retain separate, accurate, and detailed financial records and accounts. Id.
Finally, AES Corp. and its affiliates will not pledge AES Ohio’s assets or stock as collateral
for obligations other than AES Ohio’s. Id. Additionally, the TYRP Stipulation, to which the
City, OCC, and CUB Ohio are signatories, would bind AES Ohio to several provisions.
Thus, any further limitations imposed on AES Ohio’s management discretion could be
redundant and unnecessarily restrictive. Lastly, we remind parties that the Ohio Revised
Code paired with the Commission’s own administrative rules create a robust regulatory
framework regarding AES Ohio’s affiliate transactions (R.C. 4928.17), corporate separation
practices (Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-37), governance of asset transfers and change in utility
control (R.C. 4905.28 and 4905.402), and maintenance of separate bookkeeping as reviewed
by the Commission (R.C. 4903.03 and Ohio Adm.Code 4901:1-37-04(B)). Notably, Joint
Applicants have stated they will abide by all applicable laws and Commission regulations
governing AES Ohio’s operations, and they are legally obligated to do so.

       {¶ 41}   The Commission is also convinced by Joint Applicants’ explanation that,
because an objective of the Transaction is to ensure the maintenance of an investment grade
credit rating for AES Ohio, excessive dividends as a result of the Transaction would be
incompatible. Thus, while we do not dispute the importance of concerns regarding the
balancing of customers’ needs with financial gains that might result from the Transaction,
we are satisfied by Joint Applicants’ representations—as verified by Staff—and determine
that the concerns are either addressed in this proceeding or can be addressed in other
pending cases. However, to facilitate sound decision-making amongst AES Ohio’s Board of
Directors, the Commission orders that any board members who have pecuniary interests in
data centers shall recuse themselves from all decision-making regarding issues related to
data centers. Therefore, considering the Application and proposed Merger Plan, recent AES
Ohio merger precedent and conditions, intervenors’ comments, and public input, the

Commission determines that the Transaction will promote public convenience and result in
the provision of adequate service for a reasonable rate, rental, toll, or charge.

       {¶ 42}   Moreover, while we observe several requests for a public hearing in this
proceeding, we find that the relevant information and comments from intervening parties,
the public, and elected officials have provided ample grounds to reach an informed decision
regarding the pending Application. As summarized above, the Commission heard direct
public feedback regarding the Transaction during the local public hearings held for the
TYRP Proceeding. Moreover, while CCRRD specifically requests a “local hearing” to create
a record for cross-examination, we emphasize that regardless, a local public hearing would
not have been the proper venue to build out such a record. It appears that CCRRD is
conflating the purpose of local public hearings and evidentiary hearings. The Commission’s
local public hearings are first and foremost forums for the public to voice their opinions
regarding cases. We have received and considered such input regarding the Application
and proposed Merger Plan. As such, we find that a local public hearing and evidentiary
hearing, in addition to the comments filed in this case and statements taken during the TYRP
Proceeding, are not necessary and would serve only to unduly prolong our consideration of
the Application. We also note that this is procedurally consistent with similar acquisition
cases brought before the Commission. 2024 Merger Case, Finding and Order (Mar. 5, 2025)
¶ 29 (Commission determined a hearing was unnecessary); In re Joint Application of Cinergy
Corp., et al., Case No. 05-732-EL-MER, Finding and Order (Dec. 21, 2005) ¶ 12 (determination
that a hearing was unnecessary, as the comments presented enough information to be
considered); In re Vectren Energy Delivery of Ohio, Case No. 26-33-GA-UNC, Finding and
Order (June 24, 2026) ¶ 26; In re Vectren Energy Delivery of Ohio, Case No. 18-1027-GA-UNC,
Finding and Order (Jan. 30, 2019) ¶ 14.

       {¶ 43}   Therefore, the Commission determines that Joint Applicants propose a
transaction that will promote the public convenience and result in the provision of adequate
service for a reasonable rate pursuant to R.C. 4905.402(B). Additionally, we impose the
directive made in Paragraph 41 and adopt the Staff Report’s recommendation that AES Ohio
